title: America.gov, the government's new assistant, scores level with GPT-5.5
paragraphs: America.gov, which says it answers questions with AI and information from government websites, scores {agovExact}% on PolicyBench. GPT-5.5, which OpenAI released in April, matches that score with AI alone and no web access, while GPT-6 Sol leads at {solExact}%, also with AI alone. America.gov would rank #{agovRank} of {nRanked}, but PolicyBench keeps its board to AI alone. PolicyBench counts a dollar amount as right when it falls within $1 of the reference PolicyEngine computes, and an eligibility answer as right when it matches. It weights each answer by household impact.

The General Services Administration has run America.gov since September 29. Between October 14 and 18, PolicyBench sent each of its {households} households to America.gov in a new chat, with the board's own prompt in the JSON answer format. It scored every reply as it scores the board. Six prompts run past the {charLimit} characters America.gov asks a message to stay within, so PolicyBench split each across two chats asking for half the outputs apiece. Before publishing a run, PolicyBench asks again whenever a board model leaves answers out. America.gov got the same kind of retry: PolicyBench sent each refused prompt again, word for word, in a fresh chat, up to twice. On first attempts alone, America.gov gets {agovFirstExact}% (#{agovFirstRank}).

America.gov refused prompts for {firstRefusalHouseholds:words} households the first time it saw them. "I cannot estimate or calculate federal or state tax, credit, payroll, or benefit amounts," it replied to the prompt for a Virginia single parent of two. When PolicyBench asked again, America.gov answered {answeredOnRetry:words} of those prompts in full and repeated its refusal word for word on the other {refusedThrice:words}, which leaves {unansweredRate}% of its scored answers blank. Of the {nModels} models on the board, {fullModels} answer every one.

On income taxes, America.gov falls between GPT-5.5 and GPT-6 Sol: it gets {fedTaxRate}% of federal amounts within $1, against their {gpt55FedTaxRate}% and {solFedTaxRate}%, and {stateTaxRate}% of state amounts, against {gpt55StateTaxRate}% and {solStateTaxRate}%. It trails both on SNAP amounts and Medicaid eligibility. On SNAP it gets {snapRate}%, against {gpt55SnapRate}% and {solSnapRate}%, and it put a Michigan couple's SNAP at ${snap072} a year, where PolicyEngine and {snap072Models} of the {nModels} models give $0. On Medicaid eligibility, which PolicyBench weights most heavily, it gets {medicaidRate}%, against {gpt55MedicaidRate}% and {solMedicaidRate}%. It called both adults in a New York couple eligible, where PolicyEngine and {medicaid004Models} models find neither eligible.

The board's prompts name PolicyEngine, the open-source tax and benefit model behind the references, in {peOutputs:words} output definitions. They ask about Medicaid and CHIP eligibility "under PolicyEngine rules," and ask "whether PolicyEngine returns" support for free and for reduced-price school meals. PolicyBench is revising that wording. At least {peRefusals:words} of America.gov's {firstRefusals:words} refusals cited PolicyEngine, and no model on the board declined a household on that ground. On the answers each gave, America.gov leads GPT-5.5 on {peLeads:words} of those {peOutputs:words} outputs and trails it by at most {peMaxGap} points on the others. If PolicyBench left all {peOutputs:words} out for every model, America.gov would rank #{noPeRank} of {nRanked}.

America.gov's terms say the answers it generates with AI "can be incomplete or wrong." PolicyBench tested America.gov once and skipped the last retry it gives board models, in which it asks again, one at a time, for each answer still missing. If PolicyBench ran that retry, it would need at least {rowRepairChats} more chats, and America.gov could rise to {rowRepairMaxRate}% at most.

data.label: Script that scores them the board's way
